Cuban Engineers

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Does South Africa really need help from Cuban water engineers to solve our pressing water problems?

Unique Selling Point:
Last month Minister Sisulu welcomed 24 Cuban engineers to the country, who are said to bring valuable international expertise to our engineers and municipal workers. At a cost of R64million, these "experts" will mentor locals as the Department once again tries to find a magic bullet to fix the countries water woes. This is not the first time Cuban experts come to assist the DWS. In 2014/15 we also got help from the country, but many are sceptical that these imports add any real value to our current situation.

Summary:
Local engineers, water experts and even trade unions are criticising the Minister's latest move to bring in so-called water experts from Cuba. In a time when unemployment is skyrocketing in the country many feel that the R64 million rand could have been spent on local experts and businesses. Not only does our economy need some stimulation, but many agree that South Africa has some of the best water experts and engineers in the world. We have enough engineers and they certainly fall within the government's budget. So why has DWS opted for outside help. On top of that people are sceptical about the Cubans' expertise and training. South Africa has unique challenges and a very unique hydrology.

Further information:
It is said that South Africa loses about 1.5 million m³ water every year, equating to between 7 and 9 billion rand due to failing water infrastructure. The Department of Water and Sanitation has been very aware of these figures, especially in recent times of drought. Over the past decade various measures were implemented/discussed or even initiated to try and help save water, whether it be better recycling and treatment of wastewater, protecting existing water sources from pollutants, addressing infrastructure failures... etc...
But the fact is that even today most of our cities and towns are facing huge problems with water. As residents of a big city like Johannesburg we may not realise the crisis staring at us, but if you step back and look at the bigger picture, you will realise that every day there is a water cut somewhere, pipes are bursting, sometimes at regular spots, where the pressure is high or the infrastructure has become particularly weak.
More than a decade ago we were warned that the day will come when we no longer have assurance of supply, when there is no longer a guarantee that water will come from your tap when you turn it on. We're there. Partly because our water is no longer enough to reach us all, but also because a lot is wasted and poorly recycled and treated.
The DWS's latest rescue initiative lies in the hands of 24 Cuban water engineers. Min Sisulu welcomed them at a lavish event last month. They are said to mentor our municipal workers and to transfer skills to our municipal engineers, who are apparently in short supply.
According to the Department this is a great opportunity to learn from these Cuban experts, many of whom cannot speak English. Economist Xhanti Payi says in light of SA's critics engineering skills shortage we should embrace their willingness to share their knowledge, and that it is standard practice for any growing company to bring in foreign expertise.
But there has been a local outcry. Trade Union Solidarity has begun legal proceedings against the Department stating that they could easily supply local engineers to fulfil those positions. The Cuban engineers come at a cost of R64m... besides their “stipends” there are additional costs like accommodation, transport, translators etc involved.
On top of that the engineers are not registered in South Africa, and to date ECSA has not confirmed whether or not it will in fact register the engineers. Cuba is not a signatory to the Washington Accord, so no Cuban engineer has an internationally recognised certification. This means that no international financial institution will fund anything designed by a Cuban engineer. Cuba's water system is in disarray and their water sector is primitive. They only supply about 60% of their population with water. Having said that, that in itself does not make them unimportant. South Africa, for example has a health system with a bad reputation, yet our medical experts are highly sought after overseas.
On top of that we have a high unemployment rate in South Africa. We have unemployed engineers that are for some reason overlooked by the Department. We have engineers looking for work internationally because they cannot find work in SA. The deployment of the Cuban engineers is said to erode what is left of our technical capacity.

Press Release:


The Cuba-South Africa relationship goes back to the late 1990s when it was decided to exchange technical skills and training as a tangible expression of the South African government’s commitment to supporting an ideological ally. The bilateral agreement has seen South African students study medicine in Havana and Cuban doctors deployed in government hospitals in this country, while military mechanics have been helping to maintain military equipment for the SANDF. The cooperation has come at a great cost to the South African taxpayer, and the Department of Water and Sanitation’s latest importation of 24 Cuban engineers to assist in urgent maintenance of municipal infrastructure in far-flung rural provinces has spurred legal action to try and stop the move. Carte Blanche investigates what’s at stake for unemployed local engineers.

Script:


CUBAN ENGINEERS SCRIPT


V/O
14”
With South Africa’s water infrastructure stretched to breaking point after years of poor maintenance, Minister of Water and Sanitation, Lindiwe Sisulu welcomed 24 Cuban water engineers to the country at the end of April.
Sisulu
You come at a time when we sorely need you. You come at a time when we would like to give your people hope.
V/o
8:17”
Each engineer will earn about R700,000 a year and a R65 million budget is set aside for the programme over three years.
Link
South Africa has a long history with Cuba dating back to the liberation struggle. At a time when the South African government shunned the ANC, Cuba stepped in with considerable support.
V/O
7”

It’s all part of an old relationship that you can’t put a price-tag on, says political scientist Dr Piet Croucamp..
Piet
Don't quantify what's happening. What you have to think is that it's a relationship, and the relationship must have some operational features, some cooperative features. The Cubans, they have engineers, they have health care professionals in primary health care. And that's the level where the cooperation makes the most sense.
V/O
6:08”
Water strategist, Prof Anthony Turton warned of imminent collapse in water management for years.
Turton
The water sector is in an advanced stage of collapse as a result, particularly of cadre deployment and the purging of skills from the water services value chain. And as a result of that, we probably down to about 20 percent of the capacity that we had maybe in 1994.
V/O
7:18”
But for local engineers, the thought of Cubans brought in to fix a problem they can, while their own work dwindles, is painful.
Sifiso
We’ve been asking ourselves, why is our government actually taking for granted our profession?
V/O
11”
Mechanical engineer Sifiso Vezi started his own firm in Durban in 2006. He specialises in water infrastructure engineering - but his work has dried up.
Sifiso
Looking at my qualifications, I was very sure that it would be easy for me to actually get the work. And I must say that when I started, it was relatively easy. But now we’re just living from hand to mouth.
V/O
15”
His company that once employed over 200 people is now run on skeleton staff and even his son, Njabula, a qualified civil engineer, is now looking for employment elsewhere. That’s why Vezi opposes the Department’s decision.
Sifiso
It hit home when I see my boy every day looking for employment. And he is a damn good engineer.
Vishaal
We have many civil engineers, both junior and senior civil engineers, that remain unemployed or even not having full time employment.
V/O
14”
Vishaal Lutchman is the CEO of the South African Institution of Civil Engineering. SAICE promotes growth and sustainability in the industry. Of their 14,500 members, over a 1000 are unemployed.
Vishaal
Derek: I would assume that many of our qualified civil engineers who are unemployed are feeling hot under the collar now.

Yes, I think that this event has exposed that. However, I think that the frustrations are a long time coming.
V/O
18:15”
This is not the first time Cuban engineers have come to assist the Department. Former Director General of Water Affairs, Prof Mike Muller was part of the first South African contingent that went to Havana in 2002 to negotiate the initial water cooperation agreement between the two countries.
Mike Muller
I think it was the right thing to do at the time. It worked quite well.

Derek: Is still a good idea now?

Look, in the early 2000s, we actually did have a shortage of personnel. The wonderful thing in twenty years is that the universities have produced hundreds of qualified engineers, many of whom can't be professionally registered because they can't get the right experience.
Link
There’s no doubt that there are many qualified yet unemployed engineers in the country, especially in these Covid times. The obvious question is… why isn’t the government using them?
Leonardo
Derek: Can you understand why there's an outcry from qualified engineers who are out of work?

Of course, and that is the reason why we are actually participating as far as the Infrastructures South Africa’s initiatives are concerned, unblocking of the bigger projects to stimulate the economy.
V/O
13”
Acting Deputy Director general for Infrastructure at the Department of Water and Sanitation, Leonardo Manus, says the Department has been supporting local engineers and the Cubans will not compete in the job market.
Leonardo
In total, we have spent close to 10 billion in this financial year stimulating the private engineering sector, and we believe we can do even more.
LINK
Most of us in Suburbia don’t think much about water, we turn on a tap and it’s there. But South Africa’s unique hydrology compared with the fact that we get far less than average global rainfall means that it’s a complicated and expensive infrastructure to get this water all the way from the Lesotho highlands to here….
V/O
7”
While the Department of Water and Sanitation is custodian of the country’s water, municipalities do the delivery.
Mike Muller
Local government is responsible for the water supply and sanitation services, and they should be pushed to do the job better. But it's their job. They have the money. And if they use the money they had properly, we could do a lot better than we're doing at the moment.
V/O
7”
And this is where the Department sees the Cuban role - as support for some of the most vulnerable municipalities.
Leonardo
They came to complement. They came to augment as far as the desire of the department is concerned in that space of the expertise that they have…

Derek: We've got the experts doubting their qualifications.

Well, we have subjected their qualifications to our own regulatory authority in that space, which is Sakwa. And it was confirmed as to be acceptable and so there was no need for the department to doubt their qualifications.
Turton
You must remember that Cuba has been under comprehensive economic sanctions since the Bay of Pigs and Cuban Missile Crisis. So if anything, what the Cubans know how to do is they know how to keep old broken machinery still going. They’re kind of famous for that. But they are not famous for water services management for the simple reason that only about 60 per cent of the total Cuban population today is serviced with good quality, safe drinking water.
Leonardo
Cuba doesn't really have a sophisticated water supply system. So how will they contribute?

Well, it might not be sophisticated as far as the advances in high-end technology in some areas in the country are concerned, but nor do South Africa have sophisticated engineering assets all across the country. When there's something that is highly advanced that need to be designed to Cuban engineer cannot design that for you and we will not expect them to design that for you. But as far as maintaining what we have, they can actually give great input into that regard in terms of our maintenance planning management.
V/O
15:07”
The plan is for the Cubans to mentor the Department’s Learning Academy graduates at more outlying and rural municipalities, where the need is greatest - partly because the department says South Afican engineers don't want to work in remote areas.
Vishaal
We don't agree with that. We think engineers, engineers by by nature work in remote locations.
Sifiso
I’ve never advertised a job which is in those far flung areas and an engineer says, I'm not going there. We will go anywhere as long as the remuneration is right.
Manus
Are we talking about engineering companies that needs to be appointed to do certain projects? Because, yes, we find engineering companies to actually do those projects in the most remote of areas … or is it engineers that are willing to come and work in the department?

Derek: But you're not paying enough.

Well, we are working according to the laws of this country, as well as the public service, what the Public Service Act tell us to do, and we ruminate accordingly.
Piet
Derek: But looking at it practically for a moment. Do you think they can help our water situation?

You don't have to be Einstein to fix South Africa's water problem. The infrastructure is just not being maintained. The Cubans will make no difference to that. It might alleviate in pockets of areas some of the pressure that exists because of the poor infrastructure but we don't have the money to make the difference.
Turton

The last accurate numbers I saw was that we need something like 900 billion rand just to fix what is broken in the water sector.
Mike
You know, we can plan for what we would love to have or we can plan for what we've got with the resources that we have. If used properly, we could fix lots of the problems that we have.
Derek: How do we move forward on the water and sanitation issue?

The professional associations are trying to encourage the use of skills and the proper management of the skills we have. We’ve got to strengthen our organisations starting with that local municipality in the Eastern Cape, all the way up to a Rand Water Board, or the national Department.
V/O
12”
While the trade union Solidarity is taking the Minister to court to try and put a stop to the Cuban deployment, engineers like Vezi and his son, are feeling desperate about their future...
Sifiso
Derek: How do the young engineers like your son feel about the Cuban engineers?
They've just lost hope and even my son was supposed to be here, but he said daddy this won’t help. But for me, even in my head, maybe I won't be an engineer for long. I think I'll just venture into business wherever that takes me…



END

PROMO 1
Minister Lindiwe Sisulu’s decision to bring in water experts from Cuba has been met with considerable opposition. Why are we importing skills when South African engineers are unemployed?
PROMO 2
In a time of rife unemployment and economic hardship, government has opted to invest in Cuban skills to help rescue our water sector. Why have local experts been sidelined?
PROMO 3
Can 24 Cuban water engineers make a real difference to our collapsing water sector, and why opt for foreign expertise when our own engineers are desperate for work?

The wonderful thing in twenty years is that the universities have produced hundreds of qualified engineers, many of whom can't be professionally registered because they can't get the right experience. Link There’s no doubt that there are many qualified yet unemployed engineers in the country, especially in these Covid times. The obvious question is… why isn’t the government using them? Leonardo Derek: Can you understand why there's an outcry from qualified engineers who are out of work? Of course, and that is the reason why we are actually participating as far as the Infrastructures South Africa’s initiatives are concerned, unblocking of the bigger projects to stimulate the economy. V/O 13” Acting Deputy Director general for Infrastructure at the Department of Water and Sanitation, Leonardo Manus, says the Department has been supporting local engineers and the Cubans will not compete in the job market. Leonardo In total, we have spent close to 10 billion in this financial year stimulating the private engineering sector, and we believe we can do even more. LINK Most of us in Suburbia don’t think much about water, we turn on a tap and it’s there. But South Africa’s unique hydrology compared with the fact that we get far less than average global rainfall means that it’s a complicated and expensive infrastructure to get this water all the way from the Lesotho highlands to here…. V/O 7” While the Department of Water and Sanitation is custodian of the country’s water, municipalities do the delivery. Mike Muller Local government is responsible for the water supply and sanitation services, and they should be pushed to do the job better. But it's their job. They have the money. And if they use the money they had properly, we could do a lot better than we're doing at the moment. V/O 7” And this is where the Department sees the Cuban role - as support for some of the most vulnerable municipalities. Leonardo They came to complement. They came to augment as far as the desire of the department is concerned in that space of the expertise that they have… Derek: We've got the experts doubting their qualifications. Well, we have subjected their qualifications to our own regulatory authority in that space, which is Sakwa. And it was confirmed as to be acceptable and so there was no need for the department to doubt their qualifications. Turton You must remember that Cuba has been under comprehensive economic sanctions since the Bay of Pigs and Cuban Missile Crisis. So if anything, what the Cubans know how to do is they know how to keep old broken machinery still going. They’re kind of famous for that. But they are not famous for water services management for the simple reason that only about 60 per cent of the total Cuban population today is serviced with good quality, safe drinking water. Leonardo Cuba doesn't really have a sophisticated water supply system. So how will they contribute? Well, it might not be sophisticated as far as the advances in high-end technology in some areas in the country are concerned, but nor do South Africa have sophisticated engineering assets all across the country. When there's something that is highly advanced that need to be designed to Cuban engineer cannot design that for you and we will not expect them to design that for you. But as far as maintaining what we have, they can actually give great input into that regard in terms of our maintenance planning management. V/O 15:07” The plan is for the Cubans to mentor the Department’s Learning Academy graduates at more outlying and rural municipalities, where the need is greatest - partly because the department says South Afican engineers don't want to work in remote areas. Vishaal We don't agree with that. We think engineers, engineers by by nature work in remote locations. Sifiso I’ve never advertised a job which is in those far flung areas and an engineer says, I'm not going there. We will go anywhere as long as the remuneration is right. Manus Are we talking about engineering companies that needs to be appointed to do certain projects? Because, yes, we find engineering companies to actually do those projects in the most remote of areas … or is it engineers that are willing to come and work in the department? Derek: But you're not paying enough. Well, we are working according to the laws of this country, as well as the public service, what the Public Service Act tell us to do, and we ruminate accordingly. Piet Derek: But looking at it practically for a moment. Do you think they can help our water situation? You don't have to be Einstein to fix South Africa's water problem. The infrastructure is just not being maintained. The Cubans will make no difference to that. It might alleviate in pockets of areas some of the pressure that exists because of the poor infrastructure but we don't have the money to make the difference. Turton The last accurate numbers I saw was that we need something like 900 billion rand just to fix what is broken in the water sector. Mike You know, we can plan for what we would love to have or we can plan for what we've got with the resources that we have. If used properly, we could fix lots of the problems that we have. Derek: How do we move forward on the water and sanitation issue? The professional associations are trying to encourage the use of skills and the proper management of the skills we have. We’ve got to strengthen our organisations starting with that local municipality in the Eastern Cape, all the way up to a Rand Water Board, or the national Department. V/O 12” While the trade union Solidarity is taking the Minister to court to try and put a stop to the Cuban deployment, engineers like Vezi and his son, are feeling desperate about their future... Sifiso Derek: How do the young engineers like your son feel about the Cuban engineers? They've just lost hope and even my son was supposed to be here, but he said daddy this won’t help. But for me, even in my head, maybe I won't be an engineer for long. I think I'll just venture into business wherever that takes me… END PROMO 1 Minister Lindiwe Sisulu’s decision to bring in water experts from Cuba has been met with considerable opposition. Why are we importing skills when South African engineers are unemployed? PROMO 2 In a time of rife unemployment and economic hardship, government has opted to invest in Cuban skills to help rescue our water sector. Why have local experts been sidelined? PROMO 3 Can 24 Cuban water engineers make a real difference to our collapsing water sector, and why opt for foreign expertise when our own engineers are desperate for work?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Does South Africa really need help from Cuban water engineers to solve our pressing water problems?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Last month Minister Sisulu welcomed 24 Cuban engineers to the country, who are said to bring valuable international expertise to our engineers and municipal workers. At a cost of R64million, these "experts" will mentor locals as the Department once again tries to find a magic bullet to fix the countries water woes. This is not the first time Cuban experts come to assist the DWS. In 2014/15 we also got help from the country, but many are sceptical that these imports add any real value to our current situation.
metadata.Summary: Local engineers, water experts and even trade unions are criticising the Minister's latest move to bring in so-called water experts from Cuba. In a time when unemployment is skyrocketing in the country many feel that the R64 million rand could have been spent on local experts and businesses. Not only does our economy need some stimulation, but many agree that South Africa has some of the best water experts and engineers in the world. We have enough engineers and they certainly fall within the government's budget. So why has DWS opted for outside help. On top of that people are sceptical about the Cubans' expertise and training. South Africa has unique challenges and a very unique hydrology.
metadata.Further information: It is said that South Africa loses about 1.5 million m³ water every year, equating to between 7 and 9 billion rand due to failing water infrastructure. The Department of Water and Sanitation has been very aware of these figures, especially in recent times of drought. Over the past decade various measures were implemented/discussed or even initiated to try and help save water, whether it be better recycling and treatment of wastewater, protecting existing water sources from pollutants, addressing infrastructure failures... etc... But the fact is that even today most of our cities and towns are facing huge problems with water. As residents of a big city like Johannesburg we may not realise the crisis staring at us, but if you step back and look at the bigger picture, you will realise that every day there is a water cut somewhere, pipes are bursting, sometimes at regular spots, where the pressure is high or the infrastructure has become particularly weak. More than a decade ago we were warned that the day will come when we no longer have assurance of supply, when there is no longer a guarantee that water will come from your tap when you turn it on. We're there. Partly because our water is no longer enough to reach us all, but also because a lot is wasted and poorly recycled and treated. The DWS's latest rescue initiative lies in the hands of 24 Cuban water engineers. Min Sisulu welcomed them at a lavish event last month. They are said to mentor our municipal workers and to transfer skills to our municipal engineers, who are apparently in short supply. According to the Department this is a great opportunity to learn from these Cuban experts, many of whom cannot speak English. Economist Xhanti Payi says in light of SA's critics engineering skills shortage we should embrace their willingness to share their knowledge, and that it is standard practice for any growing company to bring in foreign expertise. But there has been a local outcry. Trade Union Solidarity has begun legal proceedings against the Department stating that they could easily supply local engineers to fulfil those positions. The Cuban engineers come at a cost of R64m... besides their “stipends” there are additional costs like accommodation, transport, translators etc involved. On top of that the engineers are not registered in South Africa, and to date ECSA has not confirmed whether or not it will in fact register the engineers. Cuba is not a signatory to the Washington Accord, so no Cuban engineer has an internationally recognised certification. This means that no international financial institution will fund anything designed by a Cuban engineer. Cuba's water system is in disarray and their water sector is primitive. They only supply about 60% of their population with water. Having said that, that in itself does not make them unimportant. South Africa, for example has a health system with a bad reputation, yet our medical experts are highly sought after overseas. On top of that we have a high unemployment rate in South Africa. We have unemployed engineers that are for some reason overlooked by the Department. We have engineers looking for work internationally because they cannot find work in SA. The deployment of the Cuban engineers is said to erode what is left of our technical capacity.
